claim: CLC transporter proteins catalyze coupled exchange of chloride (Cl–) for protons (H+).
source: CLC transporter proteins are present in intracellular compartments throughout our bodies – in our hearts, brains, kidneys, livers, muscles, and guts – where they catalyze coupled exchange of chloride (Cl–) for protons (H+) (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jentsch and Pusch, 2018

claim: Knockout animals lacking CLC transporters exhibit severe neurodegeneration and osteopetrosis.
source: Their physiological importance is underscored by phenotypes observed in knockout animals, including severe neurodegeneration and osteopetrosis (Sobacchi et al., 2007; Stobrawa et al., 2001; Hoopes et al., 2005; Kasper et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on knockout animals

claim: CLC transporters are linked to human diseases including X-linked mental retardation, epileptic seizures, Dent's disease, and osteopetrosis.
source: by their links to human disease, including X-linked mental retardation, epileptic seizures, Dent's disease, and osteopetrosis (Lloyd et al., 1996; Hoopes et al., 2005; Veeramah et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking CLC mutations to human diseases

claim: CLC-ec1 is a prokaryotic homolog that has served as a paradigm for the CLC family.
source: CLC-ec1 is a prokaryotic homolog that has served as a paradigm for the family (Estévez et al., 2003; Lin and Chen, 2003; Engh and Maduke, 2005; Miller, 2006; Matulef and Maduke, 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations establishing CLC-ec1 as a model system

claim: CLC-ec1 enables resistance to acidic conditions such as those found in host stomachs.
source: Its physiological function enables resistance to acidic conditions, such as those found in host stomachs (Iyer et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iyer et al., 2003

claim: CLC-ec1 is a homodimer in which each subunit contains an independent anion-permeation pathway.
source: Like all CLC proteins, CLC-ec1 is a homodimer in which each subunit contains an independent anion-permeation pathway (Miller and White, 1984; Ludewig et al., 1996; Middleton et al., 1996; Dutzler et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations establishing the dimeric structure

claim: Gluex acts both as a gate for Cl– transport and as a participant in H+ transport.
source: Gluex is positioned at the extracellular entryway to the Cl–-permeation pathway, where it acts both as a 'gate' for the transport of Cl– and as a participant in the transport of H+ (Dutzler et al., 2003; Accardi and Miller, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Gluex function

claim: Gluin appears to act as a H+ transfer site.
source: Gluin is located towards the intracellular side of the protein and away from the Cl–-permeation pathway, where it appears to act as a H+ transfer site (Accardi et al., 2005; Lim and Miller, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Gluin function

claim: In WT CLC-ec1, Gluex occupies the extracellular anion-binding site Sext in the 'middle' conformation.
source: The 'middle' conformation is observed in the WT CLC-ec1 structure, where Gluex occupies the extracellular anion-binding site, 'Sext' (Dutzler et al., 2002; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1B showing the structure

claim: When Gluex is mutated to Gln, the side chain moves upward away from the permeation pathway, allowing Cl– to bind at Sext.
source: The 'up' conformation is seen when Gluex is mutated to Gln, mimicking protonation of Gluex; here, the side chain moves upward and away from the permeation pathway, allowing a Cl– ion to bind at Sext (Dutzler et al., 2003; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1B

claim: In cmCLC, Gluex plunges downwards into the central anion-binding site Scen in the 'down' conformation.
source: The 'down' conformation is seen in the eukaryotic cmCLC structure, where Gluex plunges downwards into the central anion-binding site, 'Scen' (Feng et al., 2010; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1B

claim: Raising [H+] causes conformational change in regions of CLC-ec1 up to ~20 Å away from Gluex.
source: In previous work, we used a spectroscopic approach to evaluate conformational changes in CLC-ec1, and we found that raising [H+] (to protonate Gluex) caused conformational change in regions of the protein outside of the permeation pathway, up to ~20 Å away from Gluex (Elvington et al., 2009; Abraham et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous spectroscopic studies

claim: The H+-induced conformational state represents an 'outward-facing open' state that facilitates anion transport to and from the extracellular side.
source: Using a combination of biochemical crosslinking, double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy, functional assays, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we concluded that this H+-induced conformational state represents an 'outward-facing open' state, an intermediate in the transport cycle that facilitates anion transport to and from the extracellular side (Khantwal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study using multiple methods

claim: The QQQ mutant structure was determined at 2.6 Å resolution.
source: The structure, determined at 2.6 Å resolution (Table 1), reveals an unanticipated change in the conformation of the mutated Gluex residue, Q148 (Glnex).
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 1 showing crystallographic data

claim: In the QQQ structure, Q148 (Glnex) adopts an 'out' conformation within the hydrophobic core of the protein.
source: Instead of occupying the 'up' position, as seen in the structure of the E148Q protein (Dutzler et al., 2003), the sidechain has moved away from the permeation pathway and into the hydrophobic core of the protein, a conformation we designate as 'out' (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: The 'out' conformation of Gluex resembles the conformation in the CLC-1 channel structure.
source: This conformation, which has not previously been observed in the CLC transporters, resembles the conformation of Gluex in the CLC-1 channel structure (Park and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to CLC-1 structure

claim: Small adjustments in residues 186, 190, 199, and 357 accommodate Glnex occupancy in the hydrophobic core.
source: However, our new structure reveals that small adjustments in residues 186, 190, 199, and 357 suffice to accommodate Glnex occupancy in the hydrophobic core (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The QQQ structure reveals an opening of the extracellular vestibule, increasing accessibility from the extracellular solution to the anion-permeation pathway.
source: Analysis of the QQQ structure using HOLE, a program for analyzing the dimensions of pathways through molecular structures (Smart et al., 1996), reveals an opening of the extracellular vestibule, increasing accessibility from the extracellular solution to the anion-permeation pathway, in contrast to previously described structures.
evidence: Supported by HOLE analysis of the structure

claim: In WT CLC-ec1, two sub-Angstrom bottlenecks occur between Scen and the extracellular side of the protein.
source: In the WT protein, two sub-Angstrom bottlenecks occur between Scen and the extracellular side of the protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by HOLE analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: In the QQQ protein, the extracellular bottlenecks are relieved, widening the pathway to roughly the size of a Cl– ion.
source: In the QQQ protein, these bottlenecks are relieved, widening the pathway to roughly the size of a Cl– ion (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by HOLE analysis shown in Figure 2A and Video 1

claim: The E148Q single point mutation relieves only one of the two extracellular bottlenecks.
source: In contrast, a single point mutation at the Gluex position (E148Q) relieves only one of the two bottlenecks (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by HOLE analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: The extracellular bottleneck to anion permeation is formed in part by Helix N.
source: The extracellular bottleneck to anion permeation is formed in part by Helix N, which together with Helix F forms the anion-selectivity filter (Dutzler et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to structural study

claim: Generation of the outward-facing open state involves movement of Helix N in conjunction with Helix P to widen the extracellular bottleneck.
source: Previously, we proposed that generation of the outward-facing open state involves movement of Helix N in conjunction with its neighbor Helix P (at the dimer interface) to widen this bottleneck (Khantwal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous proposal

claim: Helix N motions have been inferred from experiments on the mammalian antiporter CLC-4.
source: In addition, Helix N motions have been inferred from experiments on the mammalian antiporter CLC-4 (Osteen and Mindell, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study

claim: Disease-causing mutations in Helix N are found in CLC-1, CLC-Kb, CLC-5, and CLC-7.
source: Disease-causing mutations in Helix N are also found in CLC-Kb, CLC-5, and CLC-7 (Konrad et al., 2000; Leisle et al., 2011; Lourdel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on disease mutations

claim: Structural alignment of the QQQ mutant with E148Q or WT confirms the movement of Helices N and P.
source: Structural alignment of the QQQ mutant with either E148Q (Figure 2B–D) or WT (Figure 2D) confirms the movement of these helices.
evidence: Supported by structural alignment data shown in Figure 2B-D

claim: The structural changes in QQQ involve shifts in highly conserved residues F190, F199, and F357.
source: These structural changes involve shifts in highly conserved residues near the anion-permeation pathway, including F190 (Helix G), F199 (Helix H), and F357 (Helix N).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: The side chains of all repositioned residues in QQQ show good electron density.
source: The side chains of all repositioned residues show good electron density (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electron density maps shown in figures

claim: In QQQ, the intracellular constriction formed by S107 and Y445 is unchanged compared to WT CLC-ec1.
source: In QQQ, this intracellular constriction is unchanged compared to WT CLC-ec1 and is narrower than that observed in the CLC-1 channel (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3

claim: QQQ and E148Q bind Cl– with similar affinities (Kd = 138 ± 26 µM and 116 ± 6 µM, respectively).
source: We found that QQQ and E148Q bind Cl– with similar affinities (Kd = 138 ± 26 µM and 116 ± 6 µM, respectively) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 4A

claim: QQQ Cl– transport rates are ~2 fold faster than E148Q transport rates at pH 7.5.
source: Experimental measurements revealed that QQQ Cl– transport rates are ~2 fold faster than E148Q transport rates at pH 7.5, the pH at which the binding studies were performed (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by flux assay measurements shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: Transport rates of E148Q increase by 2-fold at pH 4.5.
source: Consistent with this prediction, transport rates of the E148Q mutant increase by 2-fold at pH 4.5 (Figure 4D; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by flux assay measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: E148Q and QQQ transport Cl– slowly compared to WT CLC-ec1 (~300 s−1 versus 2200 s−1).
source: We note that the relatively slow Cl– transport by both E148Q and QQQ compared to WT CLC-ec1 (~300 s−1 versus 2200 s−1) is not surprising, given that these Gluex mutants lack a negatively charged carboxylate to compete Cl– out of the permeation pathway.
evidence: Supported by comparison of transport rates

claim: Comparison of QQQ to WT CLC-ec1 using difference distance matrices confirms a hot spot of conformational change at Helices K-N.
source: Overall, comparison of QQQ to WT CLC-ec1 using the difference distance matrices confirms a hot spot of conformational change at Helices K-N (as illustrated in Figure 2) and highlights additional changes at G, H, I, and Q (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by difference distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Comparison of single-Glu mutant structures to WT reveals only minor (≤0.8 Å) changes.
source: In contrast, comparison of single-Glu mutant structures to WT reveals only minor (≤0.8 Å) changes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by difference distance matrix analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: CLCs are comprised of pairs of inverted structural repeats.
source: CLCs, like many secondary active transporters, are comprised of pairs of inverted structural repeats (Duran and Meiler, 2013; Forrest, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies

claim: In the QQQ structure, the inverted topology repeats have not interconverted.
source: However, the repeats have not interconverted (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: A cross-link between residue 399 on Helix O and 432 on Helix Q inhibits transport through coupling to the inner gate.
source: This region is of mechanistic interest because a cross-link between residue 399 on Helix O and 432 on Helix Q is known to inhibit transport through coupling to the inner gate (Basilio et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to cross-linking study

claim: In QQQ, residues 399 and 432 do not change position with respect to one another and do not couple to movement at the inner gate.
source: Interestingly, although we find that Helices O and Q move with respect to the rest of Repeat 2, residues 399 and 432 do not change position with respect to one another and do not couple to movement at the inner gate (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–D

claim: In WT CLC-ec1, Helix O is kinked at a conserved glycine residue G393; in QQQ, the helix is straight.
source: In WT CLC-ec1, the helix is kinked at this glycine; in QQQ, the helix is straight (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3E,F

claim: Helix H is one of the most highly conserved regions of CLC-ec1.
source: Helix H is of mechanistic interest because it contains the Gluin residue that is thought to transfer H+ from the intracellular solution to Gluex (Accardi et al., 2005; Accardi, 2015) and because Helix H is one of the most highly conserved regions of the protein (Dutzler et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural and functional studies

claim: The outward movement of Helices G-I provides space for Glnex to move to the 'out' position.
source: This outward movement provides space for Glnex to move to the 'out' position (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: The movement of Helices G-I releases the interaction between residue 113 and Glnin.
source: This movement releases the interaction between residue 113 (Helix D) and Glnin (Helix H) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: In QQQ, Glnin moves into the hydrophobic core of the protein, to within 6 Å of Glnex.
source: Strikingly, Glnin moves into the hydrophobic core of the protein, to within 6 Å of Glnex (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 6F

claim: WT CLC-ec1 exhibits pH-dependent changes in inter-subunit distance distributions for spin labels positioned on Helix N, O, P, or G.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, spin labels on Helices N and O exhibited pH-dependent changes in distance distributions in the direction predicted by the QQQ structure (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by DEER measurements shown in Figure 7B-D

claim: QQQ CLC-ec1 DEER measurements show little to no pH dependence and have distance distributions similar to those observed with WT at low pH.
source: At all three positions, the DEER distance distributions showed little to no pH dependence, and they resembled the distributions observed with WT at pH 4.5 (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by DEER measurements shown in Figure 7B-D

claim: Water spontaneously enters the hydrophobic core of WT CLC-ec1 and transiently forms water wires connecting Gluex and Gluin.
source: In our previous studies on WT CLC-ec1, extended MD simulations revealed that water spontaneously enters the hydrophobic core of the protein and transiently and repeatedly forms water wires connecting Gluex and Gluin (Han et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MD simulation studies

claim: In QQQ MD simulations, water penetration into the hydrophobic core is greatly increased, and water pathways directly connect bulk water to Glnex without requiring intermediate connection to Glnin.
source: Analogous simulation of the QQQ mutant revealed a dramatic and unanticipated result: water penetration into the hydrophobic core of the protein is greatly increased, and water pathways directly connect bulk water in the intracellular solution to Glnex, without requiring intermediate connection to Glnin (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 8A-C

claim: Water pathways in QQQ simulations were observed frequently during the 600-ns simulation (36.5% occurrence).
source: These water pathways were observed frequently during our 600-ns simulation (Figure 8D, Video 2, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1); in contrast, such water pathways were not observed in our previous 400-ns WT simulations (Han et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 8D and Video 2

claim: The occurrence of water pathways in the QQQ simulation (36.5%) is over an order of magnitude greater than the occurrence of water wires between Gluin and Gluex in the WT simulation (1.3%).
source: Moreover, the occurrence of water pathways in the QQQ simulation (36.5%) is over an order of magnitude greater than the occurrence of water wires between Gluin and Gluex in the WT simulation (1.3%).
evidence: Supported by comparison of MD simulation data

claim: Most water pathways in QQQ simulations (96%) occur when Glnin is rotated away from its starting conformation.
source: Most of the water pathways (96% of pathways observed) occur when Glnin is rotated away from its starting conformation (Clusters 1–3), allowing water to flow along a pathway near Q113 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Video 3).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: All water pathways in QQQ simulations involve rotation of E202 away from its starting position.
source: The observation that all water pathways involve rotation of E202 away from its starting position (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2, Figure 8—figure supplement 3), can explain why bulky mutations at this position would interfere with H+ transport.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation analysis shown in figures

claim: E203A can pump H+ with a non-titratable residue at the Gluin position.
source: With an Ala residue at the Gluin position (E203A), we observed clear H+ pumping above the background signal; by comparison, in line with conventional modeling, the Gluex mutant E148Q exhibited H+ signals similar to control vesicles (Figure 9B,C; Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by H+/Cl– flux assay measurements shown in Figure 9B,C

claim: The coupling stoichiometry of E203A is somewhat degraded compared to the WT protein.
source: While the coupling stoichiometry of E203A is somewhat degraded compared to the WT protein (Figure 9D), the thermodynamic fact arising from this experiment is that H+ pumping occurs with a non-titratable residue at Gluin.
evidence: Supported by stoichiometry measurements shown in Figure 9D

claim: E203Q can pump H+ but its coupling stoichiometry is substantially more degraded (Cl–/H+~75) than E203A.
source: As with E203A, we found that E203Q can pump H+; however, its coupling stoichiometry is substantially more degraded (Cl–/H+~75, Figure 9—figure supplement 1; Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by H+/Cl– flux assay measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: Double mutants E113A/E203A and E113K/E203T retain H+ pumping.
source: We also examined double mutants, missing titratable residues at both E203 and its hydrogen-bonding partner E113. When these positions are substituted with two alanines, or with the residues found in the cmCLC homolog (Thr and Lys), H+ pumping is retained (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by H+/Cl– flux assay measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: A titratable site at the Gluin position is not an absolute requirement for H+ pumping.
source: While E203Q has a severely degraded coupling ratio, it retains the ability to pump H+ (Figure 9—figure supplement 1); thus, a titratable site at the Gluin position is not an absolute requirement for H+ pumping.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from measurements

claim: The loss of coupling efficiency upon mutation of E203 is not due to loss of a H+-transfer site but rather due to an effect on the efficiency of water-pathway formation or some other aspect of the transport cycle.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the loss of coupling efficiency upon mutation of E203 (and D278 and K131) is not due to loss of a H+-transfer site but rather due to an effect on the efficiency of water-pathway formation or on some other aspect of the transport cycle.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and comparison with other mutants

claim: CLC channels operate as 'broken' transporters.
source: Compelling rationale for the close connection between CLC transporter and channel mechanisms was made over a decade ago (Miller, 2006), with CLC channels proposed to operate as 'broken' transporters.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 2006

claim: At least some CLC channel homologs retain the ability to transport H+ as part of the gating cycle.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that at least some channel homologs retain the ability to transport H+ as part of the gating cycle (Lísal and Maduke, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study

claim: The QQQ mutant was crystallized in the lipidic cubic phase without any antibody Fab fragment.
source: The QQQ mutant (E148Q/E203Q/E113Q) was crystallized in the lipidic cubic phase, without any antibody Fab fragment.
evidence: Describes the crystallization method used

claim: The QQQ structure has a space group of I222.
source: Space group	I222
evidence: Crystallographic data from Table 1

claim: The QQQ structure has unit cell dimensions of a=80.97 Å, b=120.44 Å, c=122.57 Å.
evidence: Crystallographic data from Table 1

claim: The QQQ structure was refined to Rwork/Rfree values of 0.192/0.262.
source: Rwork/Rfree	0.192/0.262
evidence: Crystallographic refinement statistics from Table 1

claim: The final QQQ model contained all residues except those of Helix A due to lack of density.
source: The final model contained all residues except those of Helix A due to lack of density for this region of the protein.
evidence: Description of the final structural model

claim: Helix A is observed in different conformations in monomeric versus dimeric CLC-ec1 structures and has no impact on function.
source: Helix A is observed in different conformations in the monomeric versus dimeric CLC-ec1 structures, and has no impact on function (Robertson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The QQQ structure represents a viable representative for a transporter intermediate based on the maintained intracellular constriction.
source: This maintained intracellular constriction supports QQQ as a viable representative for a transporter intermediate.
evidence: Based on inference from structural comparison

claim: The widening of the extracellular vestibule in QQQ predicts that Cl– transport through QQQ will be faster than through E148Q if extracellular gate-opening is a rate-limiting step.
source: The widening of the extracellular Cl– entryway in QQQ (Figure 2) predicts that Cl– transport through QQQ will be faster than through E148Q, if extracellular gate-opening is a rate-limiting step.
evidence: Based on inference from structural data

claim: Lowering pH to allow E148Q to adopt the QQQ-like conformation should increase the Cl– transport rate.
source: If this difference in transport rates is due to the wider extracellular Cl– entryway in QQQ compared to E148Q, then lowering the pH – to allow E148Q to adopt the QQQ-like (outward-facing open) conformation – should increase the Cl– transport rate.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and functional data

claim: E148Q CLC-ec1 undergoes an opening of the extracellular vestibule at low pH.
source: These results support the conclusion that E148Q CLC-ec1 (and by extension WT CLC-ec1) undergoes an opening of the extracellular vestibule at low pH.
evidence: Based on inference from pH-dependent transport rate measurements

claim: The slow Cl– transport by E148Q and QQQ compared to WT is due to the lack of a negatively charged carboxylate to compete Cl– out of the permeation pathway.
source: We note that the relatively slow Cl– transport by both E148Q and QQQ compared to WT CLC-ec1 (~300 s−1 versus 2200 s−1) is not surprising, given that these Gluex mutants lack a negatively charged carboxylate to compete Cl– out of the permeation pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from mechanistic understanding

claim: The Helix-O motions involved in transition to the outward-facing state are distinct from those postulated to facilitate inner-gate opening.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the Helix-O motions involved in transition to the outward-facing state are distinct from those postulated to facilitate inner-gate opening.
evidence: Based on inference from structural analysis

claim: Many disease-causing mutations occur in the Helix O-Q segment in both CLC channels and transporters.
source: While the mechanistic details linking Helix O-Q movements between outward- and inward-facing states are currently unknown, it is of interest to note that many disease-causing mutations occur in this segment, in both CLC channels (Saviane et al., 1999; Pusch, 2002; Bignon et al., 2020) and transporters (Lourdel et al., 2012; Veeramah et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on disease mutations

claim: Mutation of a highly conserved glycine residue in Helix O can cause Dent's disease (CLC-5) or Bartter syndrome (CLC-Kb).
source: In Helix O, for example, mutation of a highly conserved glycine residue occurring mid-helix can cause Dent's disease (CLC-5, Smith et al., 2009) or Bartter syndrome (CLC -Kb, Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to disease mutation studies

claim: The movement of Helices G-I relative to Repeat 2 provides space for Glnex to move to the 'out' position.
source: This outward movement provides space for Glnex to move to the 'out' position (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: The change in Glnin position is accompanied by a rearrangement of water molecules in the internal core.
source: This change is accompanied by a rearrangement of water molecules in the internal core (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The DEER distance distributions provide strong support for the conclusion that the QQQ structure represents a WT CLC-ec1 conformation.
source: Taken together, the DEER distance distributions provide strong support for the conclusion that the QQQ structure represents a WT CLC-ec1 conformation.
evidence: Based on inference from DEER spectroscopy data

claim: Water wires can transiently bridge Gluex and Gluin in WT CLC-ec1, which may serve as the pathway for H+ transfer.
source: Previous computational studies indicated that water wires can transiently bridge the Gluex and Gluin residues separated by 12.8 Å in the CLC-ec1 WT structure, which may serve as the pathway for H+ transfer (Wang and Voth, 2009; Han et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous computational studies

claim: The number of water molecules in pathways connecting Glnex to bulk water in QQQ simulations follows a normal distribution with chains of 5 or 6 water molecules predominating.
source: The number of water molecules needed to reach bulk water follows a normal distribution, with chains of 5 or six water molecules predominating (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 8D

claim: The majority of water wires connecting Gluex to Gluin in WT simulations involved seven or more water molecules.
source: In contrast, the majority of water wires connecting Gluex to Gluin in the WT simulation involved seven or more water molecules (Han et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MD simulation studies

claim: The absence of water pathways in WT simulations is likely due to steric hindrance by Gluin, E113, and bulky side chains.
source: The absence of water pathways in the WT simulation is likely due to steric hindrance by Gluin, E113, and bulky side chains in the vicinity, which together block direct access of intracellular bulk water toward the protein interior (despite the conformational flexibility of Gluin [Wang and Voth, 2009]).
evidence: Based on inference from structural analysis and citation

claim: The predominant water pathway observed in QQQ simulations is roughly parallel to the Cl– permeation pathway.
source: The predominant water pathway observed in our simulations is roughly parallel to the Cl– permeation pathway (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Mutations that add steric bulk at E202 or A404 inhibit the H+ branch of the CLC-ec1 transport cycle.
source: In the previous studies, mutations that add steric bulk at either E202 (Lim et al., 2012) or the adjacent A404 (Han et al., 2014) were found to inhibit the H+ branch of the CLC-ec1 transport cycle.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous mutagenesis studies

claim: Bulky mutations at E202 would interfere with H+ transport because all water pathways involve rotation of E202 away from its starting position.
source: The observation that all water pathways involve rotation of E202 away from its starting position (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2, Figure 8—figure supplement 3), can explain why bulky mutations at this position would interfere with H+ transport.
evidence: Based on inference from MD simulation data

claim: While Gluin facilitates water pathways, it is not required as a direct H+-transfer site.
source: This finding strongly suggests that while Gluin facilitates water pathways, it is not required as a direct H+-transfer site.
evidence: Based on inference from MD simulation observations

claim: The conventional thinking of Gluin as a H+-transport site must be re-evaluated.
source: Thus, the conventional thinking of Gluin as a H+-transport site must be re-evaluated.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing H+ pumping without titratable Gluin

claim: In the original study by Accardi et al., only the Gluin mutant E203Q completely abolished detectable H+ transport among 10 mutants tested.
source: In the original pioneering study by Accardi et al., Gluin was identified as a H+-transfer site following a mutagenesis scan of titratable residues at the intracellular side of CLC-ec1 (Accardi et al., 2005). Of the 10 mutants tested, only the Gluin mutant E203Q completely abolished detectable H+ transport.
evidence: Supported by citation to the original study

claim: H+ pumping was not detected in E203Q in the original study, but this is not surprising given its substantially degraded coupling stoichiometry.
source: Therefore, it is not too surprising that H+ pumping was not detected in the original study.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of current and previous results

claim: The updated transport model is compatible with transporters that have non-titratable residues at Gluin and E113.
source: Our proposed updated transport model (Figure 10A), in addition to retaining key features based on previous models (Miller and Nguitragool, 2009; Feng et al., 2012; Basilio et al., 2014; Khantwal et al., 2016), unifies our picture of both CLC transporter and channel mechanisms. First, it is compatible with transporters that have non-titratable residues at Gluin and E113.
evidence: Based on inference from simulations and experiments

claim: The Gluin and E113 residues play a key role in regulating water pathways rather than in direct hand-off of H+.
source: Our simulations and experiments (Figures 8 and 9) lead to the conclusion that these residues play a key role in regulating water pathways rather than in direct hand-off of H+.
evidence: Based on inference from MD simulations and experimental data

claim: The evolution of non-titratable residues at Gluin or E113 positions is sensible from the perspective that these residues regulate water pathways.
source: From this perspective, the evolution of non-titratable residues in either (Feng et al., 2010) or both (Phillips et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012) of these positions is perfectly sensible.
evidence: Based on inference from mechanistic understanding and citations

claim: The structural positioning of T269 in cmCLC matches the positioning of Glnin in QQQ such that side-chain dynamics could facilitate comparable water pathways.
source: Strikingly, the structural positioning of T269 in cmCLC, located at the Gluin sequence position, matches the structural positioning of Glnin in the QQQ mutant, such that side-chain dynamics could facilitate comparable water pathways (Figure 10B).
evidence: Based on structural comparison shown in Figure 10B

claim: An 'out' position for Gluex had been proposed to be essential to the mechanism of F–/H+ exchangers.
source: Previously, an 'out' position for Gluex had been proposed to be essential to the mechanism of F–/H+ exchangers (Last et al., 2018), which allow bacteria to resist fluoride toxicity (Stockbridge et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous proposals

claim: The 'out' conformation of Gluex is a unifying feature of CLC channels and transporters.
source: Thus, this conformation is a unifying feature of CLC channels and transporters.
evidence: Based on inference from structural observations across CLC family members

claim: All CLC proteins act via a 'windmill' mechanism in which protonated Gluex favors the core while deprotonated Gluex favors the anion-permeation pathway.
source: Moreover, this conclusion connotes that all CLC proteins act via a 'windmill' mechanism (Last et al., 2018), in which the protonated Gluex favors the core of the protein while the deprotonated Gluex favors the anion-permeation pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from structural data and citation

claim: The 'windmill' mechanism is preferable to previous 'piston'-type mechanisms that required protonated Gluex to compete with Cl– ions.
source: Such a mechanism is preferable to previous 'piston'-type mechanisms, with Gluex moving up and down within the anion-permeation pathway, which required a protonated (neutral) Gluex to compete with negatively charged Cl– ions.
evidence: Based on inference from mechanistic considerations

claim: One proposal is that the inner-gate area remains static and transport works via a kinetic barrier to Cl– movement.
source: One proposal is that the inner-gate area remains static and transport works via a kinetic barrier to Cl– movement to and from the intracellular side (Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous proposal

claim: Multiscale kinetic modeling revealed that 2:1 Cl–/H+ exchange can arise from kinetic coupling alone without large protein conformational change.
source: Consistent with this proposal, multiscale kinetic modeling revealed that 2:1 Cl–/H+ exchange can arise from kinetic coupling alone, without the need for large protein conformational change (Mayes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to modeling study

claim: An alternative proposal is that CLCs visit a conformationally distinct inward-open state based on cross-linking studies.
source: An alternative proposal is that CLCs visit a conformationally distinct inward-open state, based on the finding that transport activity is inhibited by cross-links that restrict motion of Helix O, located adjacent to the inner gate (Basilio et al., 2014; Accardi, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to cross-linking studies

claim: The putative inward-open state appears distinct from the conformational change observed in QQQ.
source: This putative inward-open state appears distinct from the conformational change observed in the QQQ mutant, as the inter-residue distances for the cross-link pairs (399/432 and 399/259) are unchanged in QQQ relative to WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D

claim: Gluin needs to be in the protonated (neutral) state to adopt the position that allows water pathways.
source: In our current model, we propose that Gluin needs to be in the protonated (neutral) state to adopt the position that allows water pathways.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and simulation data

claim: The proposal that Gluin needs to be protonated to allow water pathways is harmonious with the hydrophobic nature of the protein core explored by Glnin.
source: This proposal appears harmonious with the hydrophobic nature of the protein core explored by the Glnin side chain and the fact that other CLC homologs use neutral residues at this position (Feng et al., 2010; Phillips et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on inference from structural observations and citations

claim: The proposal that Gluin needs to be protonated is consistent with MD simulations showing the Gluex/Gluin doubly protonated state is highly populated.
source: In addition, the proposal is consistent with MD simulations that show the Gluex/Gluin doubly protonated state is highly populated (Mayes et al., 2018) and can favor formation of water pathways under certain conditions (Ko and Jo, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MD simulation studies

claim: Simulations with glutamate side chains in the QQQ conformational state are needed to elaborate details of H+-transfer steps.
source: Nevertheless, simulations with glutamate side chains in the QQQ conformational state, together with explicit evaluation of H+ transport (Wang et al., 2018; Duster et al., 2019), are needed to elaborate details of the H+-transfer steps.
evidence: Based on speculation about future work needed

claim: The results reported here represent an essential and pivotal step toward a complete, molecularly detailed description of mechanism in CLC transporters and channels.
source: Recognizing the importance of elaborating these details, the results reported here represent an essential and pivotal step toward a complete, molecularly detailed description of mechanism in the sui generis CLC transporters and channels.
evidence: Based on inference about the significance of the work

claim: Mutations were inserted in WT CLC-ec1 using Agilent QuikChange Lightning kit.
source: Mutations were inserted in the WT CLC-ec1 protein using Agilent QuikChange Lightning kit and were confirmed by sequencing.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: For crystallization experiments, QQQ was extracted with DM and the detergent was gradually exchanged for LMNG.
source: For crystallization experiments, QQQ was extracted with DM. The detergent was gradually exchanged for lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) during the cobalt-affinity chromatography step.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The best QQQ crystals were obtained using a precipitant solution consisting of 100 mM Tris (pH 8.5), 100 mM sodium malonate, 30% PEG 400% and 2.5% MPD.
source: The best crystals were obtained using a precipitant solution consisting of 100 mM Tris (pH 8.5), 100 mM sodium malonate, 30% PEG 400% and 2.5% MPD
evidence: Description of crystallization conditions

claim: A complete dataset for QQQ was collected by merging data from three different crystals due to radiation damage.
source: Owing to radiation damage, a complete dataset was collected by merging data from three different crystals.
evidence: Description of data collection strategy

claim: Phases for the QQQ structure were obtained using PHASER with PDB ID 1ots as a search model.
source: Phases were obtained using PHASER (McCoy et al., 2007) with PDB ID 1ots as a search model.

claim: For flux assays comparing activity at pH 7.5 and 4.5, purified CLC-ec1 were first reconstituted at pH 6 then pH-adjusted.
source: For flux assays comparing activity at pH 7.5 and 4.5, purified CLC-ec1 were first reconstituted at pH 6. The samples were then aliquoted and pH-adjusted using a 9:1 ratio of sample and the adjustment buffer.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol

claim: For experiments testing H+ pumping in mutants, a pH gradient was used to ensure measured H+ transport was from pumping and not leak.
source: For experiments testing H+ pumping in mutants, a pH gradient was used to ensure any measured H+ transport was from H+ pumping and not H+ leak.
evidence: Description of experimental design rationale

claim: The QQQ mutant shows aggregation upon purification in tartrate-containing solutions.
source: Isethionate was chosen as the anion of choice for purification of proteins for the ITC experiments since the QQQ mutant shows aggregation upon purification in tartrate-containing solutions, which were previously used for ITC experiments with WT and mutant variants of CLC-ec1 (Picollo et al., 2009; Khantwal et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of experimental observation

claim: The QQQ mutant is comparatively stable in isethionate and remains stable throughout the ITC experiment.
source: The mutant is comparatively stable in isethionate and continues to remain stable throughout the ITC experiment.
evidence: Description of experimental observation

claim: DEER experiments were performed at 83 K on a Bruker 580 pulsed EPR spectrometer at Q-band frequency (33.5 GHz).
source: DEER experiments were performed at 83 K on a Bruker 580 pulsed EPR spectrometer at Q-band frequency (33.5 GHz) using either a standard four-pulse protocol (Jeschke and Polyhach, 2007) or a five-pulse protocol (Borbat et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: In the QQQ simulation, 2 Cl– ions bound at Scen and Sint sites in each subunit were preserved.
source: The 2 Cl– ions bound at Scen and Sint sites in each of the two subunits were preserved for the simulation.
evidence: Description of simulation setup

claim: The pKa of each ionizable residue in QQQ was estimated using PROPKA and protonation states were assigned at pH 4.5.
source: The pKa of each ionizable residue was estimated using PROPKA (Olsson et al., 2011; Rostkowski et al., 2011), and the protonation states were assigned based on the pKa analysis at pH 4.5.
evidence: Description of simulation setup method

claim: In the QQQ simulation, E111, E202, E235, and E414 were protonated.
source: Specifically, E111, E202, E235, and E414 were protonated in the simulation.

source: The resulting systems consisting of ~155,000 atoms were contained in a 164 × 127×98 Å3 simulation box.

claim: A 600-ns equilibrium simulation was performed for the QQQ system without any restraint applied.
source: Then a 600-ns equilibrium simulation was performed for the system without any restraint applied.

claim: In Subunit 2 of the QQQ simulation, Glnex drifted away from the 'out' position within five ns and did not return.
source: In Subunit 2 of the homodimer, Glnex drifted up and away from the 'out' position at the beginning of the simulation (within five ns), and it did not return to the 'out' position during the simulation.
evidence: Description of simulation observation
